ACT Policing sits under the AFP as the community policing arm. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP Australian police and policing ‘Staggering’: watchdog condemns police after Indigenous teenager on bus wrongfully arrested – then searched Ombudsman Iain Anderson says he is concerned police ‘had no clearly understood definition of racial profiling’ Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Adeshola Ore Mon 24 Aug 2026 10.01 EDT Last modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 10.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The commonwealth and ACT ombudsman has criticised the Australian federal police for failing to clearly define “racial profiling” after police in Canberra pulled guns on an Indigenous teenager who they mistook for a suspect in an aggravated burglary. The scathing investigation, released on Tuesday, made eight recommendations to the Australian federal police (AFP) and ACT Policing after investigating the November 2025 incident. ACT Policing sits under the AFP as the community policing arm. Court ends case against police charged over use of Taser and pepper spray on ‘vulnerable’ First Nations man Read more The 17-year-old Aboriginal boy, referred to by the pseudonym Jay in the ombudsman’s report, boarded a bus in Woden on the evening of 11 November 2025. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email ACT Police stopped the bus and three officers entered with guns drawn. After being taken off the bus at gunpoint, Jay was then brought to the ground, handcuffed and arrested, the report said. Less than 90 seconds later, police realised their mistake. Police had mistaken him for a suspect in an aggravated burglary . Police released Jay, apologised to him and searched him. He then got back on the bus to continue his journey. Police did not ask for his name, confirm his age, or ask for details to contact a family member, according to the ombudsman’s report. Iain Anderson, the commonwealth and ACT ombudsman, concluded that Jay was searched “inappropriately and seemingly unlawfully” after he was released from arrest. “One of the other police who was there said, ‘Hey, here’s an opportunity. Let’s search him anyway even though we know he’s not the person we’re looking for,” Anderson said. “It was a bit staggering for me to see that that was their approach.” The ombudsman found no evidence that Jay’s Aboriginality led to increased use of force. But Anderson said he was concerned that the AFP “had no clearly understood definition of ‘racial profiling’”. In a statement provided to the ombudsman in April, Jay’s family said what happened to him “still sits heavy with all of us”. “We felt helpless. We felt scared. We felt like we couldn’t protect him in that moment, and that’s something no family should ever have to feel,” they said. “The only way forward is for ACT Policing to truly listen, to own their mistakes, and to commit to doing better, not just for [Jay], but for all our children and future generations.” The description of the alleged offender for the burglary included the term “Aboriginal male”. Anderson said the use of “Aboriginal” as a physical descriptor was unhelpful and relied on the use of “outdated, stereotypical physical trait”. He acknowledged ACT Policing were responding to a fast-evolving incident but concluded there were opportunities to improve the force’s engagement with First Nations communities and their aftercare of “innocent people who are caught up in their actions”. “Altogether, the incident lasted just under 4 minutes. But it, and its aftermath, have had serious repercussions for Jay and his family and on the already fragile relationship between ACT Policing and the ACT’s Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities,” the report said. The report’s recommendations include that ACT Policing review its use of race as a proxy to describe a person’s physical traits and adopt objective descriptors and develop clearer guidance to support officers performing the role of “Alpha 8” to make decisions on command of an incident. Alpha 8 is a role assigned to an on-duty inspector, where they have responsibility for the strategic overview of policing resources. Both recommendations have been accepted. The AFP accepted in principle the recommendation that it establish a clearly understood definition of “racial profiling” aligned with the objectives of Australia’s Racial Discrimination Act. The ombudsman said the definition should be included in the AFP’s order on professional standards, which establishes internal guidance. The AFP said these orders were not the appropriate place to embed racial profiling. It said it would undertake a review of AFP and ACT Policing governance to determine if additional clarification would support members in applying the relevant principles. In correspondence to the ombudsman, Krissy Barrett, the AFP commissioner, said it was “committed to continuous improvement and to rebuilding trust and strengthening relations between the community and its police force.” Last year, the ACT’s chief police officer, Scott Lee, apologised for the incident and acknowledged the trauma it would have caused Jay, his family and the broader Indigenous community. Lee told the ombudsman he remained committed to building and strengthening its relationship with the ACT’s First Nations community. An Australian Army soldier has been killed and five others injured during a military exercise in the Mount Bundey training area in the Northern Territory, the Australian defence force says. Photograph: LCPL Jessica Gray/AP View image in fullscreen An Australian Army soldier has been killed and five others injured during a military exercise in the Mount Bundey training area in the Northern Territory, the Australian defence force says. Photograph: LCPL Jessica Gray/AP Australian military Australian Army soldier killed and five others injured in training exercise in the Northern Territory Defence confirmed the fatality occurred on Monday at the Mount Bundey training area, with next of kin informed Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Josh Butler Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.28 EDT First published on Mon 5 Oct 2026 18.42 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An Australian soldier has died and five others were injured in a training accident at a facility outside Darwin yesterday, according to the defence department. The department on Tuesday morning released a statement confirming the incident, which occurred at the Mount Bundey training area, around 100km south-east of Darwin in the Northern Territory. “Defence can confirm an Australian Army soldier has died during a training exercise at the Mount Bundey Training Area on 5 October 2026,” the statement read. “Five other Australian Army soldiers were injured.” The department did not immediately confirm the nature of the incident or the cause of death, saying only: “Defence will provide further updates when possible.” Guardian Australia has contacted the defence department for further information about the nature of the incident and injuries. The defence minister, Richard Marles, who is the acting prime minister, was also contacted. The department was expected to provide more details later on Tuesday. Marles in a social media post on Tuesday afternoon said the defence force had “experienced a tragic loss of one of our finest soldiers” but did not provide further details. “Australia’s service men and women do an exceptional job training and fighting for our country. This work in the defence of our nation carries risk. Our thoughts in this difficult time are with their family and friends,” he said. “Defence is currently working with and supporting all the families in this difficult time.” In a separate statement, prime minister Anthony Albanese – who is in Tuvalu for the pre-COP leaders’ meeting – also sent condolences. “There are no safe or easy days for those who serve in our country’s name. This sad incident is a terrible reminder of what families take on when their loved one bravely puts on our nation’s uniform,” he said. “Every loss and every incident is felt deeply by the broader Defence family, but by none more so than their mates who served alongside them. We think of them today and every day.” The NT’s chief minister, Lia Finocchiaro, indicated in a press conference that the incident had occurred on Monday evening. NT She said two people were evacuated by helicopter to Darwin around 7.30pm, with another three taken by plane around 9.30pm. “Our sincerest condolences to the family of the young service personnel who lost their life yesterday,” Finocchiaro said. “Our thoughts and prayers are with the family who are obviously devastated by this loss and of course the support of our entire community is there for all of our service personnel who will be feeling this loss immensely.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The NT’s police commissioner, Martin Dole, said officers had been sent to the facility to “assist defence” in responding. He also declined to provide further details but said police were “helping to investigate on behalf of the coroner”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “Next of kin has been notified. We request that the privacy of Defence members and families is respected at this time,” the department said. The incident comes following several high-profile training accidents claiming the lives of ADF personnel. Jack Fitzgibbon, the son of the former Labor defence minister Joel Fitzgibbon, died in 2024 during a parachute incident during a routine training activity in Sydney. Three separate inquiries were launched after the death of Fitzgibbon: a Comcare inquiry led by the commonwealth’s WHS regulator; a New South Wales coronial inquiry; and an internal defence probe. Lachlan Muddle, an experienced paratrooper, died in March after a mid-air collision with another trooper during training above a Jervis Bay airfield. Following Muddle’s death, Marles said the Australia defence force had been provided with recommendations from investigations into the death of Fitzgibbon. “In both that incident [2024] and this one, it is vital that investigations are as thorough as humanly possible so that every lesson is learned,” Marles said in March. The federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor, said the Coalition was awaiting further updates from the government “at the appropriate time.” “It’s another tragic reminder that our men and women warfighters put their lives on the line even when they are not on mission,” he said in a statement. “We are also thinking of the five soldiers injured in this incident. We wish them a full and swift recovery, and our thoughts are with their families who will be supporting them through this very challenging time.” Joel Fitzgibbon, in a social media post on Tuesday, sent condolences to those affected in the Mount Bundey incident. “It’s an another reminder that training exercises are a preparation for war and are risky in and of themselves.
